Sensus Divinitatis
SEN-sus div-ih-NIH-tah-tis
noun phrase (Latin theological term)
Latin sensus (sense, perception, feeling, from sentire, to feel, perceive) + divinitatis (of divinity, genitive of divinitas, from divinus, divine, from deus, god). The phrase — “sense of divinity” — was coined and formalized by John Calvin in his Institutes of the Christian Religion (I.iii.1) to describe the innate awareness of God that every human being possesses by virtue of bearing the divine image — not an inferred conclusion but an immediate, prereflective God-knowledge planted by the Creator.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The sensus divinitatis is Calvin’s term for the inborn, universal awareness of God’s existence and moral authority — the God-knowledge that is native to every human being, indelibly imprinted on the soul as part of the imago Dei. Calvin argued in the Institutes (I.iii.1) that “God Himself has implanted in all men a certain understanding of His divine majesty... this sense of divinity can never be effaced.” It is not a natural-theological inference from observation — not the cosmological or teleological argument reasoned through to a conclusion — but an immediate, intuitive awareness of deity prior to argument. Paul grounds this in Romans 1:19–20: “that which is known about God is evident within them — for God made it evident to them.” The knowledge is internal (en autois, in them), the result of divine action, not human discovery. Romans 2:15 adds the moral dimension: the Gentiles “show the work of the Law written in their hearts — their conscience also bearing witness.” This dual witness — cognitive God-awareness and moral testimony of conscience — leaves every unregenerate person “without excuse” (Rom. 1:20). The sensus divinitatis does not save; it renders every human being culpable for suppressing the truth they already hold (Rom. 1:18). In Reformed apologetics (Cornelius Van Til, Alvin Plantinga), it grounds the claim that belief in God is “properly basic” — not dependent on argument but immediate, warranted by God’s own implanting.

Webster 1828 Definition

Latin: “sense of divinity.” Calvin’s term (Institutes I.iii.1) for the innate, universal awareness of God’s existence and moral authority implanted by the Creator in every human soul prior to argument — not an inference from evidence but an immediate God-knowledge that leaves all persons without excuse.

expand to see more

SENSUS DIVINITATIS [Latin: sense of divinity] Calvin’s (Institutes I.iii.1) term for the innate universal God-awareness implanted by the Creator in every human soul — not an argument from evidence but a prereflective, immediate knowledge of God that precedes all theological reasoning.

2. Grounded in Paul: Romans 1:19–20 (“what is known about God is evident within them”) and Romans 2:15 (“the work of the Law written in their hearts”). The sensus is internal, universal, indelible, and suppressed in unbelief — not absent in the unregenerate but held down in unrighteousness (Rom. 1:18).

3. Reformed apologetics (Van Til): all men actually know God (sensus divinitatis) but suppress that knowledge; the apologist’s task is not to fill an empty cup but to expose the suppression already occurring. Alvin Plantinga (Warranted Christian Belief, 2000) formalized the claim that the sensus divinitatis produces properly basic belief in God — warranted without inference from other beliefs.

4. The sensus divinitatis does not rescue anyone: its function in redemption is to render suppression inexcusable, not to create natural pathways to salvation. That requires the Spirit’s testimony applied to the gospel.

Key Scripture

Romans 1:19 — "because that which is known about God is evident within them — for God made it evident to them."

Romans 1:20 — "For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes — His eternal power and divine nature — have been clearly seen, being understood through what has been made. So they are without excuse."

Romans 2:15 — "In that they show the work of the Law written in their hearts — their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts alternately accusing or defending them —"

Psalm 19:1 — "The heavens are telling of the glory of God — and their expanse is declaring the work of His hands."

Modern Corruption

Postmodern secular thought suppresses the sensus divinitatis by treating atheism as the intellectually neutral default and theism as an inference requiring external proof — inverting Paul’s teaching that God-knowledge is the baseline human condition and unbelief is the suppression of it.

expand to see more

The Enlightenment project adjudicated all truth claims — including God’s existence — by the bar of autonomous human reason. In this framework, God’s existence becomes a hypothesis to be proven rather than a given to be acknowledged or suppressed. Kant’s epistemology placed the noumenal (including God) beyond empirical knowledge, making religious belief a matter of practical reason rather than cognitive awareness. This inverts Calvin’s position: for the Enlightenment tradition, God-knowledge requires argument; for Paul and Calvin, it is the natural condition of the creature — not the conclusion of an argument but the starting point being suppressed. The modern academic default that atheism is the “null hypothesis” and theism bears the burden of proof is precisely the suppression of the sensus divinitatis Paul describes in Romans 1:18–21, now institutionalized as intellectual virtue.

Within progressive Christianity, the sensus divinitatis is sometimes reread as a universal religious openness — a pluralistic spiritual instinct finding God in many forms across all world religions. This “perennial philosophy” reading of Romans 1 treats Paul’s account of universal God-knowledge as evidence for a common core of world religions. Paul’s point is the opposite: the sensus divinitatis is the knowledge of the Creator that all humanity shares and suppresses, and the fact of its suppression explains why “the world by wisdom knew not God” (1 Cor. 1:21). Universal God-awareness does not confirm religious pluralism; it condemns universal religious idolatry.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin sensus (sense, perception) + divinitatis (of divinity); Calvin’s coinage names an immediate, pre-theoretical God-knowledge planted in every soul by the Creator — not the product of reasoning but the precondition of it, and the ground on which every unbeliever is inexcusable.

expand to see more

Latin sentire — to feel, perceive, be aware of; the sensus is perception, not inference — God-awareness is native to the creature, not a conclusion reached by argument

Latin divinitas — divinity, godhood, from deus (God); the genitive divinitatis specifies what the sense perceives: not a vague “sacred” but the true Creator God whose eternal power and divine nature are clearly seen (Rom. 1:20)

Greek nomos — law; Romans 2:15’s “law written in the heart” is the moral dimension of the sensus divinitatis — conscience is God’s moral awareness planted within, not a social construct external to the person

Latin imago Dei — image of God; the sensus divinitatis is part of what it means to be image-bearers — awareness of God is not incidental to human nature but constitutive of it, which is why it persists in the fallen

Latin inexcusabilis — without excuse; Calvin follows Paul: the sensus divinitatis makes every human being accountable — the knowledge of God was never absent, only suppressed — so that the unbeliever stands before God inexcusable, not ignorant

Usage

"In Reformed presuppositional apologetics (Van Til, Frame), the sensus divinitatis means the unbeliever is never a blank slate asking for proof of God: they are a knower suppressing God-knowledge, and the apologist’s task is to expose that suppression rather than to fill an empty cup with evidence."

"When someone claims “I just can’t believe in God,” the Reformed response informed by the sensus divinitatis is not “let me provide more evidence” but “what are you suppressing?” — Paul says the knowledge is already there; the question is why it’s being held down in unrighteousness."

"The sensus divinitatis distinguishes Reformed natural theology from Rome’s: Vatican I (1870) taught that unaided reason can demonstrate God’s existence; Calvin taught that the knowledge is immediate, planted, and inexcusable — not demonstrated by argument but suppressed by the sinful will."
